How Vermont property tax works

A Vermont bill has two layers: a statewide education tax and a municipal tax set by each town. The town listers set the appraised value on the grand list, and the town collects both parts.

The Department of Taxes, through its Property Valuation and Review division, oversees the system. With 247 municipalities, 237 towns and 10 cities, the bill depends heavily on where the house sits. The state sets the education rate framework, while your selectboard and voters set the municipal side.

Statewide rates and ratios

MeasureRate or ratio
Statewide common level of appraisal72.36 percent
Nonhomestead education tax rate1.391 percent
Homestead education base rate1.00 percent
Effective total rate, homestead1.66 percent
Effective total rate, nonhomestead1.70 percent

The common level of appraisal compares listed value with fair market value. At 72.36 percent, a typical house sells for more than its listed value, and the state uses that ratio to adjust education rates. It does not change the value on your own bill.

The homestead declaration

By filing a homestead declaration you tell the state this house is your domicile, and you pay the homestead education rate rather than the nonhomestead rate. Without a declaration, Vermont treats the property as nonhomestead.

The declaration is due each April 15, with October 15 as the last accepted date. A town can charge a late penalty of up to 3 percent if the nonhomestead rate is higher than the homestead rate, or up to 8 percent if it is lower. After the October deadline the property is classified as nonhomestead, and the owner pays the higher rate plus any penalty and interest.

  • As a rule you must be a Vermont resident living in your own home as a domicile on April 1.
  • A home leased more than 182 days in the calendar year, used exclusively for commercial or rental purposes, or used as a second home or camp is nonhomestead.
  • A home sold before April 1 generally can't carry a homestead declaration.

The same Form HS-122 carries the property tax credit claim. About two-thirds of homesteads receive a credit, and households with income under $47,000 may get an additional credit and a municipal credit.

How to appeal your assessment

You appeal in steps, starting with the town listers, then the board of civil authority, then the state or the Superior Court. Each step has a short deadline.

  1. Listers hear people aggrieved by their appraisals on or before May 20, and such hearings are not held later than June 2 (32 V.S.A. § 4221).
  2. After the listers' final decision, appeal in writing to the board of civil authority within 14 days after the date of notice, by lodging the appeal with the town clerk (32 V.S.A. § 4404).
  3. From the board's decision, an appeal to the Director of Property Valuation and Review or the Superior Court begins by notice within 30 days (32 V.S.A. § 4461).

The board of civil authority must hold a hearing and inspect each appealed parcel, and it may sustain, increase or decrease the listers' value. Few cases reach the state level: 36 appeals on the 2023 grand list and 19 on the 2024 grand list.

Reappraisals and your bill

Many towns are overdue, and the state is pushing them toward regular reappraisals. Act 68 requires full reappraisals every six years starting January 1, 2025, unless the Division approves a longer period.

The average last reappraisal year across the state is 2016, and 60 towns last reappraised more than 15 years ago. Towns have been booking reappraisals for 2026 through 2029.

A reappraisal can move the listed value closer to market value. Before you assume your tax bill matches what a buyer will pay, check the date of your town's last reappraisal on the town website or ask the listers.

Education tax rates ahead

The state projects that the average education property tax bill will rise by 11.9 percent in fiscal year 2027.

That percentage is a statewide average, so individual bills vary. Homestead rates depend on local education spending, and the nonhomestead rate is uniform statewide. Buyers reading the bill on a listing sheet may be looking at last year's number, so show the current bill from the town clerk or treasurer.

Current Use and what it means for a seller

Current Use, formally the Use Value Appraisal program, taxes enrolled farm and forest land on its productive use value instead of market value. It started in 1978 and now covers 19,692 parcels and 2,574,742 acres, about one-third of Vermont's land.

  • Enrolled land stays in the program after a sale unless the owner or the Division withdraws it.
  • The new owner must submit a transfer application and required documents within 30 days after the transfer is recorded.
  • Once an application is approved and recorded, a contingent lien is placed on the land.
  • If the new owner develops the land or changes its use, the land use change tax may apply, at 10 percent of the fair market value of developed land.

The 2024 use values were $188 an acre for forest land, $141 an acre for forest more than one mile from a road, and $483 an acre for agricultural land. A house on a larger wooded lot may be partly enrolled, so ask your listers whether any of your acreage is in the program before you list.

Taxes due at closing

Closing brings one main tax, the property transfer tax, payable within 30 days of the closing date. A buyer who will live in the house pays 0.5 percent on the first $200,000 and 1.25 percent beyond it, with a 0.22 percent Clean Water Surcharge on the portion over $200,000. A year-round home that won't be the buyer's principal residence and isn't a long-term rental carries 3.40 percent, or 3.62 percent with the surcharge.

Sellers who live out of state see 2.5 percent of the price withheld by the buyer, who files Form RW-171 within 30 days, unless the seller holds a Commissioner's Certificate.

Expect $15.00 per page to record a deed and a flat $15.00 for a transfer tax return. The town clerk has the current figures.

Selling with back property tax owed

Owing tax doesn't stop a Vermont sale: the unpaid amount comes out of the proceeds at closing. It still helps to know how collection works before you pick a closing date.

  • A collector may charge a commission of up to 8 percent of the tax after the deadline in the collector's notice, and voters may set a lower rate or a grace period (32 V.S.A. § 1674).
  • The collector mails a notice at least 30 days before the payment date, and if no date is set payment is due 30 days after mailing (32 V.S.A. § 4772).
  • A tax sale needs a delinquency of at least $1,500 for more than one year, and the collector must first offer a written repayment plan (32 V.S.A. § 5252).
  • The sale is advertised in a local newspaper three weeks in a row, and the delinquent owner and any mortgagee get certified-mail notice at least 30 days before the sale.

After a tax sale the owner, lienholder or mortgagee may redeem within one year by paying the sale price plus interest at 1 percent per month. Landlords selling a rental should also know that owners of rented property file a Landlord Certificate (Form LRC-140) each year.

If the back taxes are tied to a house you can't afford to fix up, an as-is cash sale can pay them off at closing.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Vermont homestead declaration due?

Each April 15, with October 15 as the last accepted date. After that, the property is classified as nonhomestead and the owner pays the higher rate plus any penalty.

How long do I have to appeal my Vermont assessment to the board of civil authority?

You have 14 days after the date of the listers' notice, and you lodge the appeal in writing with the town clerk under 32 V.S.A. § 4404.

Can I sell a house in Vermont if I owe property taxes?

Yes, the unpaid tax is paid from the proceeds at closing. A tax sale requires at least $1,500 delinquent for more than a year, and owners get a year to redeem.

Does a nonresident seller owe Vermont withholding?

Yes. The buyer withholds 2.5 percent of the sale price on Form RW-171 unless the seller holds a Commissioner's Certificate.

What is the Vermont property transfer tax rate?

For a principal residence it is 0.5 percent on the first $200,000 and 1.25 percent above, plus a 0.22 percent surcharge on the excess. Many non-principal homes pay 3.40 percent.

Who owes Vermont estate tax

Vermont charges an estate tax, but only on large estates. Under 32 V.S.A. § 7442a, an estate with a Vermont taxable estate under $5,000,000 owes nothing, and an estate of $5,000,000 or more owes 16 percent of the amount above $5,000,000.

The tax is figured on the whole estate, not on one house. Bank accounts, retirement plans, business interests and a Vermont home all add up to the total, and an apportionment fraction trims the tax to the Vermont share. Vermont charges no separate inheritance tax: nothing is measured on what an heir receives, because the tax falls on the estate before anything is handed out.

Most families inheriting a Vermont house owe no estate tax. A typical owner-occupied home here is worth $316,600, far under the $5 million line. Only heirs of larger estates, such as a house sitting beside a big investment portfolio, need a closer look.

Vermont and federal estate figures

Numbers to keep handy when an estate holds a Vermont house:

RuleAmount or deadline
Vermont estate tax threshold$5,000,000
Vermont rate above the threshold16 percent
Vermont filing threshold$5 million, matching the payment threshold
Extension of time to fileSix months, Form EST-195
Federal basic exclusion for 2026 deaths$15,000,000

The federal exclusion is higher than the Vermont threshold, so an estate can owe Vermont estate tax while owing no federal estate tax.

When an estate must file a Vermont return

Form EST-191 is required when the decedent held an interest in Vermont property and the federal gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts from the last two years before death tops $5 million, or whenever a federal Form 706 must be filed. The Legislature in 2026 raised the filing threshold to $5 million so that it matches the payment threshold.

For a resident, property located in Vermont leaves out real or tangible property outside the state. For a nonresident, intangible property is also left out. A nonresident who owned a Vermont vacation house therefore counts the house, but not the brokerage account held in another state.

An executor handles other returns too: an income tax return (IN-111) and, if the estate earns income, a fiduciary return (FIT-161). If more time is needed for the estate tax return, Form EST-195 gives six months and must be filed on or before the due date.

Federal rules for an heir who sells

For deaths in 2026 the federal estate tax exclusion is $15,000,000. A surviving spouse can elect to claim whatever part of the late spouse's exclusion went unused.

Income tax on the sale follows separate rules. The exclusion of up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, requires living in the home two of the last five years (IRS Topic 701). Heirs who never lived there rarely qualify, so their gain is worked out on its own.

Probate when the estate owns a Vermont house

If the person who died held real estate in their own name, Vermont calls for a formal estate in the Probate Division of the Superior Court, in the county where they lived. The same applies once the estate is worth more than $45,000.

The court confirms the executor named in a will or, without a will, appoints an administrator. Surviving spouses and next of kin have priority when suitable, and the personal representative generally posts a bond before appointment.

  • Inventory: due 30 days after appointment, listing assets at date-of-death fair market value.
  • Creditor notice: run in a local newspaper within 30 days of appointment. Creditors then get four months from publication.
  • The personal representative should not pay claims until the four months are up.
  • If publication is skipped and unknown creditors exist, the claim window can stretch to three years after death.

Title companies look for proof that debts and claims were dealt with, so these dates shape when a sale can close.

Can the executor sell the house?

Yes, with court permission. Before selling, conveying, mortgaging or leasing real estate, the personal representative files a Motion for License to Sell or Convey Real Estate (form 700-00035) and reports back on the license after the sale.

At closing the personal representative signs the deed in front of an authorized officer, and it is recorded with the clerk of the town or city where the house stands. It cites the license order. Once debts and expenses are paid, a decree of distribution issues, and a certified copy goes into the town land records to clear title for heirs.

Town clerks, not a county office, keep Vermont's land records. Recording runs $15.00 per page, and recording a property transfer tax return is a flat $15.00. Call the town clerk to confirm current fees.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Vermont houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Property transfer tax on an estate sale

Selling from an estate is a transfer by deed, so property transfer tax applies unless an exemption fits. Payment is due within 30 days of closing.

  • Buyer's principal residence: 0.5 percent on the first $200,000 of value, then 1.25 percent above that, plus a 0.22 percent Clean Water Surcharge on the amount above $200,000.
  • Year-round home that is neither a principal residence nor a long-term rental: 3.40 percent, or 3.62 percent with the surcharge.
  • Property not fit for year-round habitation: 1.25 percent plus the 0.22 percent surcharge.

Exemptions are listed in 32 V.S.A. § 9603. They cover transfers with no actual consideration between spouses, parent and child, or grandparent and grandchild. Your closing attorney can say whether one fits.

Nonresident heirs and sellers

A nonresident seller faces withholding: the buyer holds back 2.5 percent of the price for the Department of Taxes unless the seller has a Commissioner's Certificate. Form RW-171 and payment go in within 30 days of the transfer, and the seller takes the amount as a credit on Form IN-111.

Request the certificate through myVTax to cut or remove the withholding. You need all required Vermont returns filed, taxes paid, and paperwork showing the property's basis, such as an estate inventory for an inherited house. Out-of-state heirs should begin early so closing isn't delayed.

Flood disclosure and property tax before closing

Flood information has to reach the buyer before or with the contract. 27 V.S.A. § 380 asks the seller for the FEMA flood map (a copy or link), a statement on any flooding or flood damage during the seller's ownership, and whether flood insurance is carried or required. A seller who skips it lets the buyer back out before title or occupancy passes and sue for damages and fees.

Property tax keeps running too. Education tax rates differ for homestead and nonhomestead property, and a house not declared a homestead is taxed as nonhomestead. If no owner lived there as a domicile on April 1, it likely lands on the nonhomestead side, so ask the town how an estate-held house is classified.

Frequently asked questions

At what value does Vermont tax an estate?

Vermont taxes an estate only when the Vermont taxable estate reaches $5,000,000. The rate is 16 percent of the amount above $5,000,000, adjusted by an apportionment fraction.

Does an heir pay tax just for inheriting a Vermont house?

No. Inheriting itself is not taxed in Vermont, since the estate pays the estate tax. A later sale can still bring transfer tax, income tax or withholding.

Do I need probate before I sell an inherited house in Vermont?

In most cases, if the house was in the decedent's name alone. Owning real estate triggers a formal estate, and the personal representative may also need a court license to sell.

How long does an executor have to file the inventory?

Within 30 days of appointment, listing assets at their fair market value on the date of death.

What is the Vermont withholding rate on a nonresident seller?

2.5 percent of the sale price, reported by the buyer on Form RW-171 within 30 days of the transfer, unless the seller holds a Commissioner's Certificate.
